kyc_aml-all.title: KYC/AML – anti-money-laundering compliance for financial-services staff
kyc_aml-all.description: Six lessons on anti-money-laundering compliance under the GwG and Sec. 261 StGB: from the all-crimes approach through general due diligence and suspicious-activity reporting to enhanced due diligence for PEPs and real-world fine exposure – built for bank and fintech compliance staff.

kyc_aml-l0.title: Money laundering is no longer a niche topic: the all-crimes approach

kyc_aml-l0-s1.title: Since 18 March 2021: any unlawful act can be a predicate offense
kyc_aml-l0-s1.body: Before 18 March 2021, money laundering under Sec. 261 StGB was only punishable if the funds involved derived from an exhaustively enumerated statutory catalogue of predicate offenses – for example drug trafficking, organised crime, or certain tax offenses. The 18 March 2021 reform abolished that catalogue and replaced it with the so-called all-crimes approach: since then, any unlawful act suffices as a predicate offense from which an asset "derives" (Sec. 261(1) StGB) – a deliberate and significant expansion of criminal liability that compliance functions now have to factor into practically every business event. The sentencing framework differs clearly by mental state: intentional money laundering is punished under the basic offense of Sec. 261(1) StGB, and especially serious cases – for example commercial or gang-based commission – escalate under Sec. 261(5) StGB to six months to ten years' imprisonment. At least as important for day-to-day practice is Sec. 261(6) StGB: reckless (leichtfertig, i.e. grossly negligent) money laundering, carrying a markedly more lenient framework of up to two years' imprisonment or a fine. Ordinary negligence, by contrast, remains unpunished – someone who checks carefully but ultimately misses something is not criminally liable. This distinction between "reckless" and "ordinarily negligent" is not an academic nicety; in practice it decides whether an employee who overlooked a red flag can face criminal liability at all.

kyc_aml-l0-s2.title: 16 numbered categories decide who counts as an obligated entity at all
kyc_aml-l0-s2.body: Sec. 2(1) GwG exhaustively lists, in 16 numbered categories, who is subject to GwG duties at all: credit and financial services institutions, insurance undertakings, lawyers and notaries (only for specified transactions such as real-estate deals or company formations), tax advisors, real-estate brokers, and goods dealers are explicitly included. Journalists, physicians in private practice, and teachers do not appear on the list – a distinction that gets mixed up surprisingly often in practice. Two additional building blocks round out this baseline: first, the transparency register (Transparenzregister) under Sec. 18 et seq. GwG, which has been a genuine full register since 1 August 2021 (TraFinG) – legal persons under private law and registered partnerships must actively report their beneficial owners; the former notification fiction via the commercial register no longer suffices. Second, the specific cash-payment ban under Sec. 16a GwG (in force since 28 December 2022): when acquiring domestic real estate – including share deals in real-estate-holding companies – the consideration may not be paid in cash, crypto-assets, gold, platinum, or precious stones. A general, transaction-wide EUR 10,000 cash limit does not yet exist in Germany; that arrives EU-wide only with the Anti-Money Laundering Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 from 10 July 2027.

kyc_aml-l1.title: The five due-diligence duties and when they apply

kyc_aml-l1-s1.title: What's on the list – and what's deliberately missing
kyc_aml-l1-s1.body: Sec. 10(1) GwG bundles five general due-diligence duties that every obligated entity must fulfil for every relevant business relationship: identifying the contracting party; determining whether a beneficial owner exists and identifying them; obtaining and assessing information on the purpose and intended nature of the business relationship; checking whether the party is a politically exposed person (PEP), using appropriate, risk-based procedures; and ongoing monitoring of the business relationship, including transactions and, where necessary, the origin of the funds used. What is deliberately absent from this list is just as instructive as what's on it: automatically reporting the business relationship to the tax office is not a GwG due-diligence duty – conflating the two mixes up two entirely different legal regimes (tax law vs. anti-money-laundering compliance). These customer-level duties are supplemented by two customer-independent building blocks: identity verification under Sec. 12 GwG (official photo ID, eID, qualified electronic signature – video identification is not a defined statutory term but a practical form recognised by BaFin) and the entity's own risk analysis under Sec. 5 GwG, which identifies, assesses, and documents the money-laundering and terrorist-financing risks of its own business, independently of any individual customer.

kyc_aml-l1-s2.title: EUR 15,000, EUR 1,000, or no threshold at all
kyc_aml-l1-s2.body: The due-diligence duties from subsection 1 apply not only within ongoing business relationships but also to single, isolated transactions – depending on thresholds set out in Sec. 10(3) GwG. The general threshold is EUR 15,000: anyone carrying out a transaction of that size outside an existing business relationship must apply the full due-diligence duties. Money transfers (within the meaning of Art. 3 No. 9 of EU Regulation 2023/1113) and crypto-asset transfers, by contrast, are subject to a markedly lower threshold of EUR 1,000 – a deliberate regulatory response to the higher abuse potential of fast, often cross-border transfers. An example: a EUR 12,000 cash deposit by a walk-in customer with no existing account does not yet trigger a duty under the EUR 15,000 threshold – but a crypto transfer of only EUR 1,500 does, because it is well above the EUR 1,000 threshold. Most important for practice: every threshold becomes completely irrelevant the moment a concrete suspicion of money laundering or terrorist financing exists – due-diligence duties then apply regardless of the transaction value, and immediately, not only once a limit is reached.

kyc_aml-l2.title: The suspicious activity report: no threshold, no tipping off the customer

kyc_aml-l2-s1.title: To the FIU, without delay, regardless of amount
kyc_aml-l2-s1.body: If an obligated entity develops a suspicion that an asset derives from a criminal act, is connected to money laundering or terrorist financing, or that a contracting party has failed to disclose its beneficial owner, it must report this without delay to the Zentralstelle für Finanztransaktionsuntersuchungen (FIU) under Sec. 43(1) GwG – Germany's Financial Intelligence Unit, housed within the Generalzolldirektion (Central Customs Authority). Two features of this duty regularly surprise newcomers. First, there is no minimum transaction value. Unlike the general due-diligence duties in Sec. 10 GwG, the reporting duty has no EUR 15,000 or EUR 1,000 threshold – a suspected case involving EUR 50 is just as reportable as one involving EUR 5 million. Second, under Sec. 45(1) GwG the report must be filed electronically via the goAML portal; since 1 January 2024, all obligated entities must register there regardless of whether they ever actually file a report. Important for jurisdiction: BaFin is the supervisory authority and monitors whether institutions comply with their GwG duties – but it does not itself receive suspicious activity reports. The sole recipient of reports is the FIU.

kyc_aml-l2-s2.title: Stand still, and do not tip off the customer
kyc_aml-l2-s2.body: Two further duties follow on from the report and are easily overlooked in practice. First, the standstill duty under Sec. 46(1) GwG: a reported transaction may be executed at the earliest once the FIU or the public prosecutor's office has expressly consented, or once the third working day after the report's dispatch date has elapsed without a prohibition (Saturdays do not count as working days here). Sec. 46(2) GwG allows an exception where postponement is not possible or could obstruct criminal prosecution – the transaction may then be executed, but the report must be filed without delay afterwards. Second, the tipping-off prohibition under Sec. 47 GwG: the obligated entity may not inform the affected customer, other transaction parties, or any other third party about an intended or already-filed report – not even indirectly, for example through conspicuously stalling behaviour with a recognisable reason. Explicitly exempted are communication with authorities and, under certain conditions, group-internal sharing within the same corporate group. Disregarding either duty – executing a reported transaction early, or warning the customer – doesn't just jeopardise the report itself, it exposes the entity to liability of its own.

kyc_aml-l3.title: Enhanced due diligence: PEPs, high-risk countries, senior management

kyc_aml-l3-s1.title: Three independent triggers for enhanced due diligence
kyc_aml-l3-s1.body: Politically exposed persons (PEPs) trigger enhanced due diligence under Sec. 15 GwG, going beyond the baseline duties in Sec. 10 GwG – and that expanded circle does not stop at the PEP alone. Sec. 1(12) GwG defines who counts as a PEP (people holding prominent political, judicial, or military positions, domestically or abroad, or at international organisations); Sec. 1(13) GwG extends enhanced scrutiny to family members – spouses or registered partners, children and their partners, and parents; Sec. 1(14) GwG additionally covers persons known to be close associates, for example through joint beneficial ownership or close business relationships. All three groups are subject to the same enhanced measures. A second, independent trigger is high-risk third countries – the GwG itself contains no country list of its own. What matters exclusively is the list the European Commission sets via a delegated regulation (Sec. 15(3) No. 2 GwG); an entity's own internal list or an FIU list is not sufficient. A third, transaction-based trigger runs entirely independently of country of origin: especially complex, unusually large transactions with no apparent economic or lawful purpose (Sec. 15(3) No. 3 GwG) – a textbook layering pattern in the sense of the FATF model.

kyc_aml-l3-s2.title: Get senior management to approve first, not sign off afterwards
kyc_aml-l3-s2.body: Once an increased risk has been identified – whether through PEP status, a high-risk country, or a flagged transaction – Sec. 15(4) GwG prescribes concrete measures for PEP business relationships: before establishing or continuing the relationship, approval from a member of senior management is mandatory, appropriate measures must be taken to establish the source of wealth and of the funds used, and the relationship must be subject to enhanced ongoing monitoring. This is not a theoretical requirement: exactly this requirement – missing senior-management approval for a PEP business relationship – was part of a 2025 BaFin fine against a German credit institution, which also received a total fine in the six-figure range for further violations. A structurally similar but distinct rule applies to cross-border correspondent banking relationships under Sec. 15(3) No. 4 and (7) GwG: for respondents seated in a third country, enhanced due diligence always applies; for respondents in the EEA, only following the obligated entity's own risk assessment – in both cases including senior-management approval and a duty to ensure the respondent does not permit shell-bank accounts.

kyc_aml-l4.title: Fines: from EUR 150,000 to EUR 45 million

kyc_aml-l4-s1.title: Two fine tiers, and an AML officer as a countermeasure
kyc_aml-l4-s1.body: The GwG structures its fines in two tiers. The base tier under Sec. 56(1) GwG covers numerous administrative-offense provisions – for example violations of the risk analysis, internal safeguards, or due-diligence duties – with a framework of up to EUR 150,000 for intentional conduct and up to EUR 100,000 for reckless (leichtfertig) conduct; ordinary negligence does not trigger a fine here. The aggravated tier under Sec. 56(3) GwG applies only to serious, repeated, or systematic violations and raises the framework for most obligated entities to up to EUR 1 million, or twice the economic benefit derived from the violation, whichever is higher. For credit institutions and financial services institutions – and for natural persons in this sector – this aggravated framework rises even further, to up to EUR 5 million or 10% of total annual turnover. A key organisational safeguard against exactly these violations is the anti-money-laundering officer under Sec. 7 GwG: certain obligated entities – including credit and financial services institutions and insurance undertakings – must appoint one, plus a deputy; the officer reports directly to senior management, the appointment must be notified to the supervisory authority in advance, and the officer enjoys special dismissal protection lasting until one year after removal from office.

kyc_aml-l4-s2.title: Two real cases, two very different orders of magnitude
kyc_aml-l4-s2.body: Two recent BaFin proceedings show how differently sized the actual fines can be depending on the type of violation. On 23 January 2025, BaFin imposed a total fine of EUR 600,000 on KT Bank AG, made up of 30 individual fines of EUR 20,000 each – for inadequate internal safeguards, deficient record-keeping duties, and the missing senior-management approval for PEP business relationships already mentioned above. On 6 November 2025, BaFin announced a fine of EUR 45 million against J.P. Morgan SE – final and binding since 30 October 2025 – for failing, in numerous cases, to file suspicious activity reports on time under Sec. 43(1) GwG during the period from October 2021 to September 2022, caused by systemic deficiencies in internal control mechanisms. The size difference is instructive: the EUR 600,000 fine mainly concerned documentation and governance shortcomings, while the EUR 45 million fine concerned the delayed fulfilment of the core duty of the entire GwG system – the timely suspicious activity report. Both cases are publicly documented, final administrative decisions; as with any individual case, details can shift if new findings or appellate decisions emerge.

kyc_aml-l5.title: Where the real liability risk sits: the reporting duty and enhanced due diligence

kyc_aml-l5-s1.title: The risk isn't the KYC onboarding, it's what happens after
kyc_aml-l5-s1.body: This training ends where a GwG-obligated entity's real liability risk is greatest – not at the basic KYC onboarding of a new customer, but in suspicious activity reporting and enhanced due diligence for PEPs, high-risk countries, and flagged transactions. Comparing the two BaFin cases from the previous lesson makes this concrete: the largest single fine in this module, EUR 45 million against J.P. Morgan SE, did not arise from flawed KYC paperwork but from late suspicious activity reports under Sec. 43(1) GwG – the core duty of the entire system. The other case involved, among other things, the missing senior-management approval for a PEP business relationship under Sec. 15(4) GwG – a duty many institutions underestimate as an organisational formality, until a supervisor asks about exactly that. Both areas share a common pattern: they don't just require knowing a duty, they require executing it correctly under time pressure in a real incident – reporting without delay, without warning the customer, or bringing in senior management in time, before a PEP relationship begins. The quiz that follows therefore deliberately draws a disproportionate share of its questions from exactly these two topic areas.

kyc_aml-l5-s2.title: Two rules of thumb for a real incident
kyc_aml-l5-s2.body: A practical rule of thumb for daily work: for suspicious activity reports, every hour counts – "without delay" means without culpable hesitation, not "sometime this week", and both the standstill duty under Sec. 46 GwG and the tipping-off prohibition under Sec. 47 GwG start running the moment the suspicion arises, not after internal sign-off. For enhanced due diligence, by contrast, sequence is what matters most: senior-management approval must be obtained BEFORE establishing or continuing a PEP business relationship, not afterwards as a retroactive rubber stamp. Anyone who has internalised both rules – a reporting duty with no threshold and no delay, and enhanced due diligence with prior senior-management approval – has covered the core of what supervisory authorities actually fine in practice.
